# Turn Your Class Notes Into Practice Questions With Any AI Assistant

> **In short:** Paste your class notes into any AI assistant — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or others — and ask it to quiz you with questions drawn from your own material. It works on a phone or laptop, the free plans are enough to start, and the whole habit takes about 15 minutes.

By the end of this guide you'll have a routine you can use the night before any test: turn your notes into practice questions, answer them one at a time, and find the gaps before the real exam catches them. This works for high school, college, online courses, coding bootcamps, language classes, and professional certifications — anywhere notes exist.

## Before you start
- **Your notes** in a copyable form: a document, a Google Doc, photos of handwritten pages, or a PDF.
- **An AI assistant account** — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or any other major one. The free tier is enough.
- **A phone or laptop** with internet access.
- **About 15 minutes total** — most of that is you thinking through the answers.

## Step 1 — Gather your notes in one place
Open the folder, notebook, or app where your class material lives, and pull one chunk of it into a single, easy-to-copy window. If your notes are split across a notebook, a slide deck, and a textbook, you'll want them together so the AI sees the full picture. The chunk can be one chapter, one lecture, or one topic — just keep it focused enough that you can scroll through it in under a minute.

If your notes are handwritten, snap a few clear photos or type out the key points in a text file. **If it looks different** on your end — say you only have a printed page — photograph it once or type the headings plus a few lines of detail; the AI doesn't need every word, just enough to know what the material covers. **You'll know it worked when** your material is visible on screen and copyable (or uploadable) without hunting around.

💬 Example: One lecture's worth of typed notes, three photos of a whiteboard, or the last few hundred words of a Google Doc.

## Step 2 — Open an AI assistant and start a fresh chat
Open any AI assistant in a browser or app, and start a brand-new conversation. You'll usually see a blank chat box near the bottom of the screen, sometimes with placeholder text like "Message" or "Ask anything" — yours may say something slightly different. Type a short message so the AI has somewhere to respond, and check that the conversation history above is empty.

A clean chat matters: if the AI is already mid-conversation about something else, it may blend topics and your study questions get muddier. **If it looks different** — say you're on a phone — look for a "+" or pencil icon at the top of the screen to start a new chat, or open the sidebar menu. The major assistants all follow this pattern: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Mistral's Le Chat, DeepSeek, Perplexity, and others. **You'll know it worked when** you see an empty text box with a send button (often a paper-airplane icon).

💬 Example: Visit chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com, claude.ai, copilot.microsoft.com, or chat.mistral.ai — any of these will do.

## Step 3 — Paste your notes and ask for practice questions
Paste your notes into the chat box, then add a clear request for questions. The AI reads your material and replies with a numbered list of practice questions, usually within a few seconds. Watch the reply stream in below — you'll see questions that clearly come from your notes, not generic ones about the topic.

Be specific in your ask: how many questions, what types (multiple choice, short answer, essay), and what difficulty. **If it looks different** on your assistant — some tools let you upload files directly through a paperclip icon — use that instead of pasting, and the AI will read the file the same way. **You'll know it worked when** the AI replies with a numbered list of questions that reference details only someone who read your notes would recognize.

💬 Example: "Here are my notes on cellular respiration. Please create 10 practice questions that mix multiple-choice, short-answer, and one short essay. Start easy and get harder."

## Step 4 — Ask the AI to quiz you one question at a time
Reply in the same chat and ask the AI to walk you through the questions one at a time, then check your answer before showing the next one. This is the step that turns reading into learning — instead of seeing all the answers at once (which feels productive but isn't), you actively recall each one. The AI will give you question #1 and wait.

If your assistant dumped everything in Step 3 and you can already see the answers, you can still recover. **If it looks different** — some assistants may want to keep listing — simply type: "Stop after the first question, wait for my answer, then continue." **You'll know it worked when** you receive one question with no answer visible, and the AI is clearly waiting for your reply before going further.

💬 Example: "Great list. Now quiz me one at a time. After I answer, tell me if I'm right and briefly explain why. Wait for me before showing the next question."

## Step 5 — Save the questions and review what you missed
When you're done with the quiz, ask the AI to summarize which topics you got wrong or hesitated on, then copy that summary into your notes. Now you have a personalized weak-spots list instead of a one-off conversation. Reviewing that list the next day is what actually moves information into long-term memory — the quiz alone won't.

If your assistant doesn't summarize well, scroll back through the chat and copy any question you struggled with by hand. **If it looks different** — say you closed the tab by accident — most assistants keep your chat history under a "History" or "Chats" sidebar so you can reopen it. **You'll know it worked when** you have a short, honest list of two to five weak topics to revisit before the real test.

💬 Example: "Based on my answers, list the 3 topics I struggled with most and suggest one specific thing I should re-read in my notes for each."

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting too little context.** Three bullet points isn't enough — the AI will invent questions instead of basing them on your material. **Fix:** paste at least a full page or lecture's worth of notes.
- **Reading all the answers at once.** If the AI shows every question with its answer, you skip the recall step and the session barely helps. **Fix:** in Step 4, ask the AI to quiz you one question at a time.
- **Quizzing without reviewing the misses.** Doing the quiz and walking away leaves your weak spots exactly where they were. **Fix:** at the end, save the AI's summary of what you got wrong and re-read that section the next day.
- **Quizzing only the easy stuff.** It's tempting to ask about topics you already understand, because the answers feel good. **Fix:** specifically request harder questions, or pick the chapter you dread most.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Any time you have something to learn — a new language, a driving theory test, a hobby certification — this habit replaces rereading with active recall, which is one of the most effective study techniques researchers have measured.
- **For your work or business:** Use it to prep for a job interview, a sales call, a certification exam, or a presentation: paste your prep notes, get quizzed, find the gaps the night before.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't try to convert a whole semester tonight. Pick one chapter, one lecture, or one topic — get 5 or 10 questions out of it, answer them, and review what you missed. That's the smallest version of this habit that still works.

## Try it now
Open an AI assistant right now, paste the last page of notes you took this week, and ask for 5 practice questions. Answer them one at a time without peeking at your notes, then look at what you got wrong. That's the whole habit — and it's the one to repeat before every test.
